On this page

Editing ​

mosaic edit opens a model in your browser so you can change it, then saves it as a .tsr or composes it into a .glb, wherever you choose:

bash
mosaic edit <model.glb | model.gltf | model.tsr> [--port <n>] [--no-open]

A glTF model is converted to Mosaic first, with stable ids, so editing the same model twice names its nodes the same way. A .tsr opens as it is.

The editor ​

The page is the viewer, holding just your model: the node tree, the 3D view and the components of whatever node you select.

Moving parts in 3D ​

Click a part of the model to select it. It's tinted, outlined with a box (visible through whatever is in front of it), highlighted in the tree, and a handle appears at its centre. Drag the handle to move the part, and everything under it moves along.

KeyDoes
Wmove
Erotate
Rscale
↑select the part's parent: a click picks the smallest part under the mouse, like one bolt rather than the wheel
Escdeselect; so does clicking empty space

Selecting a node in the tree puts the handle on it too. When you let go, the node's new position, relative to its parent, is written to its core::transform. All moves go in one section of the archive, written by "mosaic edit", so they stay one clear layer on top of the original.

Editing together ​

Open the editor's address in a second tab, and the two tabs edit the same model together. A part moved in one tab moves in the other when you let go. There's no server in between: tabs of one browser on the same page talk to each other directly.

Try it here: these are two editors on a car. Click a part in one, such as a wheel or a door, drag the handle, and let go. The same part moves in the other editor, and only that part: the other editor moves what it already drew instead of drawing the car again.

Any viewer link can edit like this: add &edit to it, as in viewer/?example=ferrari&edit. Viewers with the same &channel=<name> share their moves; without one, every viewer editing that example in your browser does. Nothing is saved there: reloading starts from the example again.

  • Each tab has a name, such as tab-3f2a, shown in the status line and the tab's title. Its moves go in a section of the archive written by that name, so a saved .tsr says who moved what.
  • A tab opened later catches up. It asks the open tabs for everything done so far and applies it. If every tab is closed, the shared moves are gone; save first.
  • If two tabs move the same part, the later move wins, in every tab. "Later" means made after seeing the other one, not by the clock on the wall, so all tabs agree on the result.
  • The header counts what was edited, such as 12 edits · 3 sections · 2.4 KB: the edits made by every editor, the sections the archive keeps them in (a new one each time the editor changes), and the size of all the edits sent so far, added up. Moving one part ten times counts ten times there, though the archive keeps only its last position; hover over it for that size too.
  • Only moves are shared. Typing in the Files drawer stays in the tab where you typed it.

Under the hood, a move is an edit: an id, an author, its place in the order of edits, and the components it sets on which nodes. That's what a Mosaic section holds, so the same edits can later travel through the HTTP API instead, each published as a version, without changing anything but how they're carried.

Editing the files ​

The Files drawer underneath shows the archive as it really is: an index.json naming the nodes and their components, and one .ndjson table per component type, one value per line.

  1. Pick a file in the drawer, for example khronos::gltf::material.ndjson, and change it.
  2. Press Save in the drawer. The model is rebuilt from your edit and drawn again.

Moves you make in 3D show up in the drawer straight away. If the drawer has unsaved typing when you move something, it isn't refreshed; press Revert there before saving, or it would put the old transform back.

Writing it to disk ​

When you're happy, press one of the two buttons in the header. Each asks where to save:

ButtonSavesSuggested name
Save .tsrthe edited archive<model>.tsr
Export .glbthe edited archive, composed<model>.edited.glb

In Chrome and Edge this is the browser's save dialog, so you pick the folder and name. Firefox and Safari don't offer that dialog, so the file is downloaded instead; it asks where only if your browser is set to ask for downloads.

The buttons save your moves and what you last saved in the drawer. If the drawer still holds unsaved typing, they say so instead of saving. Reloading the page brings back what was last saved.

bash
mosaic edit car.glb
# Save .tsr    -> asks, suggesting car.tsr
# Export .glb  -> asks, suggesting car.edited.glb
bash
mosaic edit scene.tsr
# Save .tsr    -> asks, suggesting scene.tsr
# Export .glb  -> asks, suggesting scene.edited.glb
bash
mosaic pack car.glb original.tsr --stable-ids
mosaic diff original.tsr car.tsr       # only your edits

Notes ​

  • The page needs internet for three.js and the code editor, which load from a CDN. Your model never leaves your machine: the server listens on 127.0.0.1 only, and it writes nothing to disk itself. Files go only where you save them.
  • A part placed more than once (the same node under several parents) is one node with one transform, so moving it moves every copy. Clicking such a part in 3D selects the nearest part above it that is placed only once, which is usually what you meant by pointing at one copy. To move every copy, select the part in the tree.
  • Editing together needs the tabs in one browser, on the same address. Two machines, or two browsers, don't see each other's moves.
  • There's no undo yet. Move it back, or reload the page to return to what was last written.
  • Imports aren't followed. A .tsr that imports others opens on its own, showing only what it holds itself.
  • Large models are fine to view, slow to edit as text. A converted model keeps its geometry and textures in khronos::gltf::buffer.ndjson as long base64 lines. Open the smaller tables (materials, transforms, names in index.json) to make changes.
  • --port picks the port, otherwise a free one is used. --no-open prints the address instead of opening a browser.
